headline: Medium risk: kotaemon can ingest sensitive documents and APIs while risingwave has no documented write/egress path, so the main pairwise hazards are leakage and downstream misuse rather than direct conflict.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: kotaemon ingests HTML, MHTML, PDFs, DOCX, and chat transcripts, so prompt-like content can enter its workflow; risingwave has no documented ingestion path from kotaemon, but uncertainty about any shared workspace or manual bridge means I cannot rule out instruction smuggling. The pair lacks a documented shared channel, so this is below high.
conditions: IF the two agents share a filesystem, clipboard, or message queue
IF kotaemon content is copied into risingwave-facing prompts or jobs
mitigations: Disable any shared clipboard or shared folder between the agents.
Require manual review of any text copied from kotaemon into risingwave workflows.
Store kotaemon outputs in a read-only export directory.
Add a simple provenance tag to files before passing them onward.
requires-engineering: add channel-level provenance filtering between the agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: kotaemon explicitly handles API keys and broad document types, while risingwave has no documented data classes or egress, so the pairwise leakage path is mainly through shared storage or operator transfer. Because kotaemon can touch secrets and documents, any shared workspace would expose sensitive material even though risingwave itself is not documented to exfiltrate.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same workspace or export directory
IF kotaemon stores API keys or transcripts in files later opened by risingwave
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories.
Move secrets out of any shared file path.
Review kotaemon exports before importing them elsewhere.
Use per-agent service accounts with distinct credentials.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation at the orchestrator level.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: kotaemon supports multiple instances and writes to ./ktem_app_data, but risingwave has no documented filesystem write or mutable resource access in the profile. Without overlapping write surfaces or shared locks, a direct capability conflict is not evidenced; uncertainty stays low because the pairwise write path is not documented.
conditions: IF risingwave is configured to write into the same directory as kotaemon
IF an external orchestrator gives both agents write access to one mutable resource
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working directory.
Avoid concurrent writes to the same files.
Serialize any handoff through a single operator step.
Check for accidental symlinked paths before running both.
requires-engineering: add locking for any shared mutable resource.

D_cascading_error.rationale: kotaemon is a customer-support RAG system that can generate cited answers, and risingwave is a data-engineering system that could consume outputs as operational input if an operator wires them together. There is no documented verification step between them, so if risingwave treats kotaemon output as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream actions.
conditions: IF risingwave ingests kotaemon-generated text as trusted configuration or facts
IF an operator forwards kotaemon answers into a pipeline without verification
mitigations: Require human verification before any handoff.
Keep kotaemon output in draft-only status.
Add a checklist for source validation.
Limit risingwave to read-only consumption of handoff data.
requires-engineering: implement schema validation on all inter-agent inputs.

E_compliance.rationale: kotaemon handles API keys, chat transcripts, and office documents, which can include regulated or confidential data; risingwave is a data-engineering system with no documented residency or retention controls in the profile. The mismatch is not proven, but if the same sensitive data flows into both, differing handling policies could create a compliance gap.
conditions: IF regulated documents or transcripts are routed from kotaemon into risingwave
IF the two systems retain the same data class under different policies
mitigations: Classify data before passing it between agents.
Avoid routing secrets through risingwave.
Document retention expectations for both systems.
Delete temporary exports after use.
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls across both systems.
